findings.title: Duplicate downsize method definition overrides the width/height variant
findings.body: The file now defines `self.downsize` twice: once as `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` (line 145) and again as `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` (line 149). In Ruby, the second definition completely replaces the first. Any existing caller invoking `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, width, height)` (four positional arguments) will now hit the new signature, where `height` is bound to `opts`; since `height` is an Integer and not a Hash, this raises `TypeError: no implicit conversion into Hash`, or at best silently produces a broken dimensions string. The old width/height variant is dead code that can never run. Either remove it or consolidate into one signature that accepts both.

findings.title: Client-side max upload size hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring site settings
findings.body: `validateUploadedFile` previously used `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, respecting the admin-configurable `max_image_size_kb` and `max_attachment_size_kb`. It is now hardcoded to 10MB for both images and attachments. Consequences: (1) on sites where the attachment limit is lower than 10MB, the client will let users pick oversized attachment files and push the whole upload to the server only to be rejected; (2) on sites where the image limit is higher than 10MB, valid uploads are blocked client-side with a wrong error message; (3) it contradicts this PR's own purpose — large images that the server would now automatically downsize are still refused in the browser. Same issue for the hardcoded 10MB in the 413 handler at line 246, which is also shown to users for oversized attachments where the message was previously image-specific.

findings.title: Downsizing loop may exit with image still over the limit, then proceeds anyway
findings.body: The loop runs at most 5 iterations of an 80% resize, which reduces file size by at most ~67% (0.8^5), and only roughly — file size does not scale linearly with linear dimensions. An image that is more than ~3x the configured `max_image_size_kb` will still exceed the limit when the loop exits, yet the code proceeds to `Upload.create_for` with the oversized file, which will then fail with a generic server error instead of either being downsized further or rejected with a clear message. There is no check or handling after the loop for `tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`.

findings.title: In-place downsize (from == to) can corrupt the uploaded file, and failures are not detected
findings.body: `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)` uses the same path as both input and output. For animated GIFs this dispatches to `gifsicle ... --output <same file>`, and writing the output over the file being read is not a supported/safe operation and can truncate or corrupt the image. Additionally, `downsize` returns false when the `convert`/`gifsicle` invocation fails, but the return value is ignored here; if the external command fails partway through, the (possibly truncated or emptied) temp file is passed straight to `Upload.create_for`, storing a corrupted image. The loop should downsize to a distinct temp path and abort the upload (or fall back to the original) when `downsize` returns false.

findings.title: Synchronous CPU-heavy image resizing runs in the request thread with no size cap on remote URL downloads
findings.body: Two related problems: (1) the API URL-download branch now downloads up to 10MB (`FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)`) instead of the site-configured limit, and the subsequent downsize loop with ImageMagick/ImageOptim runs synchronously inside `create_upload` for `synchronous` API requests — a multi-second CPU-heavy operation blocking a web worker. (2) In the deferred path, the same heavy conversion runs in the Scheduler::Defer thread, but the tempfile was created in the request and is fine, yet the client has already been told `success_json` before the resize happens, so any downsizing failure surfaces only as an opaque MessageBus error. Consider capping the download back to a site setting and validating the downloaded size before attempting the resize.
